newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian army, police move south to quell unrest.
newsitem.headline: Albanian army, police move south to quell unrest.

text.p: (This story is based on official information. Our Tirana team is seeking clarification about how newly-introduced official restrictions on the media apply to foreign news organisations' reporting of Albania.)
Albanian soldiers and police forces were in control of the road south of Tirana to within 30 km (20 miles) of the riot-hit port of Vlore, government officials said on Tuesday.
On the first day of a nationwide state of emergency on Monday, government forces moved to secure the road after a weekend of armed unrest in towns in the south of the Balkan state.
Police set up a roadblock at the hilltop town of Koshovice, some 30 km (20 miles) north of the Adriatic port of Vlore, the interior ministry said in a statement.
Officers shot at a minivan when its driver refused to stop at the roadblock and attempted to turn back to Vlore.
"The police opened fire and the driver and two other men in the van were injured in the legs and arms," the ministry said.
"Police found three bombs inside the van," it added.
Albanian television said "terrorists" killed four people in Vlore on Monday as they attempted to hand in weapons. The report could not be independently confirmed.
Violent unrest rocked Vlore and other southern towns at the weekend when rioters stormed police and army weapons depots, seizing arms and ammunition.

Rilindja Demokratike, the newspaper of President Sali Bersiha's democratic party, said on Tuesday that some army commanders were "directly responsible" for failing to ensure the security of military installations.
It said military prosecutors would conduct an investigation. Soldiers "of all ranks" against whom there was evidence would be put on trial and risked stern punishment, the newspaper said.
Parliament issued a 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) deadline on Monday for "armed rebels" to give up their weapons or security forces would shoot them without warning.
Albanian television said police had also been given powers to shoot stone-throwers on sight and arrest anyone without valid identity papers.
A night curfew is also in force and Tirana police arrested 48 people in the capital on Monday night for failing to observe it. None was armed, the interior ministry said.

Koshovice commands a hill top about 10 km (six miles) south of Fier, where trouble broke out at the weekend. The interior ministry said residents in Fier had surrendered 1,500 weapons and a quantity of ammunition.
"It is calm in Fier," said a Justice Ministry spokesman Agim Neza.

He said tanks were trying to remove a roadblock on the outskirts of Gjirokaster to allow free access of trucks and other vehicles in and out of southern Albania's main town to ensure supplies reached the people.
The state run newsagency Ata said residents of Gjirokaster and other towns were buying foodstuffs in bulk.
Authorities said any attempts by private shop keepers to raise the price of bread, a staple in Albania, was unjustified because the country had sufficient supplies of flour.
The interior ministry said the army and police had blocked roads around Delvine, a town on a 30 km (20 mile) stretch of road between Gjirokaster and the coastal town of Sarande.
State run media reported separately on Monday that "armed gangs" had raided a naval base and seized weapons in Sarande.
In the port of Durres, police detained a 25-year old man in possession of a Scorpion automatic gun and bullets, the interior ministry said.
Another man was arrested in Lushnje, south of Tirana, for transporting bullets in his Mercedes car.
The first day of the state of emergency coincided with the election by parliament of Berisha to a second five-year term in office. Berisha's party holds 122 seats in the 140 member chamber.
